title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
shortTitle: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
summary: Kerberoasting abuses the way Kerberos issues service tickets. Any authenticated domain user may ask the Key Distribution Center (KDC) for a ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket that matches a registered service principal name (SPN), and part of the returned ticket is encrypted with the long-term key of the account running that service. An attacker holding any valid account, or captured Kerberos traffic, collects those tickets and takes the encrypted part away to crack offline, without touching the target system. Tickets issued with the older RC4 encryption are the most attractive, because they are cheapest to attack. The activity is loud in one way: a burst of TGS requests for many different SPNs from a single account, or requests for services that account never uses, stands out in domain controller Kerberos logs. Service ticket requests are constant in a large domain, so defenders baseline which accounts request which SPNs and alert on breadth and novelty. Long random service account passwords and strong encryption make the offline step impractical.

beginner.definition: Kerberoasting is when an attacker asks the domain for service tickets and then cracks them offline. In Kerberos, any logged-in user may ask for a ticket to a service. Part of that ticket is locked with the service account's password key. The attacker takes the locked part away and tries passwords until one fits. The domain sees the ticket requests, but never sees the cracking.
beginner.whyItMatters: The attacker needs only an ordinary user account, not administrator rights. The cracking happens on the attacker's own computer, where nobody can watch. If a service account has a weak password, the attacker learns it and can use it everywhere that account works. Many service accounts are old, over privileged and rarely changed. That combination makes this one of the most common ways to move from a normal user to full control.
howItWorks: A service account runs software, and the domain registers a service principal name (SPN) for it.
Any logged-in user can ask the domain controller for a ticket to that service.
Part of the returned ticket is encrypted with the service account's password key.
The attacker saves those tickets and picks the ones using weak, older encryption.
Offline, on their own hardware, they guess passwords until the ticket finally decrypts.
A cracked password then gives access to the service, and often to much more.
beginner.example: Imagine a library where any member may ask the desk for a sealed envelope about a staff member. The desk hands the envelope over, because members are allowed to ask. Inside is a riddle that only that staff member's password can solve. The member takes the envelope home and works on the riddle as long as they like. Nobody at the library can see the effort being spent. The only strange thing is one member asking for envelopes about many different staff members in a single afternoon.
takeaways: Service accounts need long random passwords, because offline cracking ignores lockouts.
Look for one account requesting tickets for many services in a short time.
Move services away from old weak encryption where you can.

objectives: Explain what a service principal name is and why it links a service to an account key.
Describe how any authenticated user can request a service ticket from the domain controller.
Explain why offline cracking of a service ticket is not stopped by account lockout.
Identify the Kerberos request patterns that indicate Kerberoasting.
List account and encryption changes that make offline cracking impractical.
